title: AI Readiness for the State Courts: A Guide for Courts
author: Andrea L. Miller · NCSC AI Readiness Workgroup

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The guide accepts the assistive, human-accountable model and materially develops it into an institutional governance framework. It specifies human final authority, workload-conscious design, participatory implementation, locally tailored controls and ongoing bias assessment, while documenting jurisdictional variation between approval-based and guideline-based policies.
qs: •   Participatory: Participatory methods should be used to inform decision making                at all stages of an AI implementation project.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The guide accepts the cluster’s core proposition that court AI requires continuing institutional supervision and meaningful human control. It materially develops that position through a concrete lifecycle-governance framework: named accountability, recurrent testing, staff and user participation, interim policies, data governance, project selection and human final authority.
qs: Personnel responsible for different phases of the AI system                lifecycle are identified and held accountable for the outcomes of the AI solutions.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition and materially extends it with court-specific operational controls: permitted-use restrictions, incident escalation, workflow integration, vendor due diligence, validation and contestability requirements, training, service-level commitments and model-change testing. These are practical safeguards rather than evidence that the measures improve outcomes.

Customizability &     Enables the tool to fit into      Ask for integration examples, open APIs, and  Integration           existing court workflows and      configuration flexibility.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The guide accepts selective, human-led deployment and materially extends the cluster with a staged court implementation framework covering workflow-first project selection, human responsibility, data governance, procurement, change management, baselines and iterative evaluation. Its low-risk pilots and post-project feedback cycles operationalise the cluster’s call for verification and operating-model redesign.
qs: As the Court gains experience implementing AI projects and fine-tunes its approach to change management, it will gradually become equipped to take on AI integrations with greater potential impacts and navigate greater potential risks.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s copilot framing by requiring human oversight, preserving human responsibility and rejecting uncritical or sole reliance on AI for legal and judicial work. It also confirms that permitted and prohibited uses vary by jurisdiction. It does not materially address comparative speed, cost or grounding performance.
qs: Generative AI tools are intended to provide                assistance and are not a substitute for judicial, legal, or other professional                expertise.
These provisions vary widely by jurisdiction, so it is not possible to provide a list of common provisions.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The guide directly supports the cluster’s principal framing of legal AI as a bounded, supervised aid: court personnel retain responsibility, must verify outputs, and may not substitute AI for professional or judicial judgment. Its approved-tool, device-control and breach-escalation examples also align with institutional security governance, while its jurisdictional caveat is consistent with the cluster’s recognition of varying rules.
qs: Generative AI tools are intended to provide                assistance and are not a substitute for judicial, legal, or other professional                expertise.

Court personnel must review their AI-generated material                for accuracy, completeness, and potentially erroneous, incomplete, hallucinated,                biased, or otherwise problematic output.

kp.k: Court AI readiness requires institution-wide lifecycle governance
kp.d: The guide offers a three-level framework for courts beginning to consider AI, implementing their first project, and incorporating post-project feedback. It presents improvements in access, fairness, efficiency, personnel experience, and public trust as conditional possibilities, not established general outcomes. Readiness encompasses organizational capacity throughout development, implementation, evaluation, maintenance, and feedback.
qs: AI Readiness means that the courts have the capacity, processes, systems, and policies in place to use AI effectively across the entire AI lifecycle:

This Guide provides information and tools to courts at three points on the spectrum of AI maturity: courts that are just beginning to consider AI, courts that have identified a specific AI project to implement, and courts that have already completed at least one successful AI implementation.

kp.k: Cross-functional governance should direct adoption and accountability
kp.d: The guide recommends formally establishing and supporting an AI governance group with decision-making authority, technical expertise, operational experience, and diverse stakeholder perspectives. Governance should set strategy and policies, authorize projects, monitor compliance, and manage bias, transparency, privacy, and accountability risks. Its governance tool proposes monthly meetings over a year to build foundational policies and capabilities.
qs: An AI governance committee provides the structure to answer “should we” and “can we” questions regarding AI.

The tool lays out a year-long process for establishing AI governance, beginning with identifying members of the AI Governance Committee and convening for monthly meetings with suggested agendas and tasks.

kp.k: Human-centered design must address remaining human work
kp.d: The guide recommends transparency, accountability, fairness, accessibility, and participatory design as court AI principles. It specifically warns against automating selected tasks without designing the work left to humans, or introducing tools that create additional work for intended beneficiaries. Personnel performing affected tasks and court users interacting with tools should help define needs, goals, success metrics, and design.
qs: Human-Centered Design
avoiding leftover design (designing technologies to automate certain tasks and leaving whatever work is leftover to the humans).
their insights should inform project needs, goals, and success metrics, as well as project design.

kp.k: Internal policies retain human responsibility for AI output
kp.d: The guide describes two approaches to interim internal policies: specifically authorized uses, with other uses prohibited, and use subject to guidelines without approval for every type of use. Reported jurisdictional policies commonly require human verification and responsibility, but their restrictions differ. The guide cautions that these examples illustrate policies in place at writing rather than permanently current law; courts should regularly reassess their policies.
qs: Under this approach, any AI uses that are not specifically approved by the court are prohibited.
Many policies include a blanket statement requiring human oversight of all AI tools and giving humans the final responsibility for decision making.
Utah: “Any use of AI-generated content is ultimately the responsibility of the person who uses it.”

kp.k: Data quality constrains responsible court AI deployment
kp.d: The guide treats data governance as a prerequisite to selecting useful applications, training effective models, measuring performance, and coordinating across jurisdictions. It recommends addressing missing and inaccurate data, standardizing incompatible systems and formats, adopting National Open Court Data Standards, and improving data literacy before specific projects begin. It also recognizes that deployed AI creates new data-governance obligations.
qs: The quality of a court’s data determines what kinds of AI innovations are possible and plays a critical role in successful implementation.
Conversely, when inaccurate or biased data are used to design or train a new AI tool, the AI may perpetuate and magnify those inaccuracies and biases.
This process should begin well before any specific AI projects are planned, and it should be maintained as an ongoing practice.

kp.k: AI literacy changes recruitment, training, and personnel evaluation
kp.d: The guide recommends role-specific definitions of AI literacy covering knowledge, critical evaluation, openness to innovation, and practical skills. Courts should establish literacy milestones, revise recruitment where entry-level literacy is needed, provide onboarding and continuing training, and evaluate literacy through personnel reviews. It explicitly allows that many roles may initially require little or no AI literacy at hiring, with requirements changing as adoption develops.
qs: AI literacy refers to the knowledge, attitudes, and skills needed to effectively interact with, critically evaluate, and responsibly use artificial intelligence systems.
There are likely many roles for which little-to-no AI literacy is needed upon hiring, especially in courts that have not yet adopted AI technologies.
Individual employees showing gaps in literacy should be supported with additional training and resources.

kp.k: First projects should prioritize low-risk, measurable workflow improvements
kp.d: The guide recommends identifying personnel and court-user pain points before choosing a technology, then evaluating candidates against strategic alignment, risk, effort savings, feasibility, measurable impact, stakeholder support, and reusability. Initial projects should favor internal back-office work rather than public-facing services or sensitive decisions such as sentencing and case outcomes, with limited integration needs and a 6-12 month implementation and evaluation horizon.
qs: By starting with a well-chosen project, courts can build confidence, demonstrate value, and lay the foundation for future AI initiatives.
Instead, focus on internal, back- office processes.
Aim for projects that can be implemented and evaluated within 6-12 months.

kp.k: Change management must accompany technical implementation
kp.d: The guide recommends early stakeholder engagement, communication about job impacts, participatory design, phased deployment, training, human oversight, and continuing feedback. It frames AI as supporting rather than replacing human expertise and recommends examining downstream workflow and personnel effects after rollout. Its comparison reports that reactive change management contributed to Cleo launch delays, whereas EVA incorporated structured change management from the outset.
qs: A critical component of AI implementation is developing a strong change management strategy.
Change can feel overwhelming.
This ad hoc approach meant that change management was reactive, rather than planned, which contributed to delays in launching the full product.

kp.k: Project evaluation must include hidden costs and verification
kp.d: Courts should specify whether AI replaces tasks or enhances human work and establish measurable success criteria before implementation. The guide recommends evaluating direct, indirect, and intangible costs alongside time, capacity, adoption, accuracy, and user experience. It cautions about duplicated work in hybrid operations and difficulties attributing gains to AI. Its separate numerical e-filing and scheduling examples are presented without identified jurisdictions or supporting study methods, unlike the named interview-based case studies.
qs: The court should articulate to what extent the AI is replacing human tasks altogether or enhancing employees’ work as part of a human-AI team.
However, these benefits must be weighed against potential risks, such as double- work during hybrid human-AI operations and challenges in accurately attributing improvements to the AI intervention.
To evaluate AI projects, both quantitative and qualitative metrics are important.

kp.k: Build-or-buy decisions depend on specialization and sustained capacity
kp.d: The guide generally favors purchasing solutions for generalist tasks and considering custom development for court-specific analysis where skilled personnel, suitable data, and ongoing resources exist. Buying can accelerate deployment and reduce maintenance burdens but introduces vendor dependence and customization limits; building offers control but increases cost, staffing requirements, and potential liability. For generative AI, the guide recommends hybrid approaches rather than courts building their own underlying systems.
qs: Generalist AI tasks are often better suited for buying pre-existing software solutions.
Specialist AI tasks may often be better suited for building custom solutions in-house.
we strongly recommend that courts do not attempt to build their own GenAI systems.

kp.k: Procurement must protect judicial control against vendor dependency
kp.d: The guide recommends court-specific due diligence covering vendors, investors, subcontractors, security, integration, explainability, validation, support, and full costs. Contracts should preserve court ownership of data, restrict reuse, provide appropriate source-code access and documentation, establish audit and exit rights, and require advance disclosure and testing of model changes. These are recommendations to adapt to applicable law, not a statement that every court already has these protections.
qs: Courts are bound by constitutional duties to their constituents that many technology vendors are not accustomed to navigating in their own work, and AI can require a greater dependency of the court on the vendor.
Claims of accuracy, efficiency, or time savings must be backed by data.
Vendors must not use this data for model training, resale, or analytics without express, written permission.
Unannounced changes could introduce bias, degrade performance, or violate legal constraints.

kp.k: Post-project feedback should reshape court policies and workflows
kp.d: The guide recommends completing an institution-wide feedback process before beginning another AI project. Governance structures, principles, internal policies, data practices, literacy requirements, implementation methods, and downstream work should all be reconsidered. Courts that skipped foundational readiness steps should address those omissions before further deployment. This is an iterative organizational-development framework rather than a one-time technology acquisition model.
qs: From this point forward, AI integration in the court should be an iterative process, alternating between implementing new technologies and making updates across the court system that reflect those innovations.
Each item on the checklist should be addressed before the court begins to implement the next AI project.
Have there been any unforeseen or unaddressed impacts on personnel, such as the need to reallocate their time to new types of tasks?

kp.k: EVA supports staff formation through centralized procedural knowledge
kp.d: The Orange County case study, based on an interview with Darren Dang, describes an internally built chatbot addressing turnover and procedural knowledge gaps: approximately 50% of entry level staff were new to their role or had less than two years in it. EVA retrieves answers from curated documentation, cites sources, and expanded from civil procedures to criminal, probate, family law, and juvenile domains. Reported benefits include faster staff readiness, more consistent service, and updated procedures, but no formal ROI analysis or quantified outcome estimates are supplied. Public-facing and multilingual services remain envisioned extensions.
qs: EVA is designed to retrieve accurate answers from a curated knowledge base using natural language queries.
The court did not conduct a formal return-on-investment (ROI) analysis
The project revealed that many procedures were outdated or inconsistent, prompting a renewed focus on regularly reviewing and updating documentation.
Although it currently serves internal users, the court envisions expanding EVA to public- facing services

kp.k: EVA adoption depends on content maintenance and behavioral support
kp.d: The EVA account attributes adoption to operational stakeholder involvement, incremental testing, Microsoft Teams integration, training, promotional activity, leadership support, and nudges to consult the chatbot before supervisors. Subject matter experts reviewed response feedback and updated the knowledge base. The account characterizes technical maintenance as relatively limited, with most sustained effort devoted to current procedural content; expectations of quick ROI for other organizations are prospective judgments rather than measured findings.
qs: Most of the long-term effort involves keeping the knowledge base current
staff were encouraged to consult EVA before asking supervisors, and supervisors were prompted to redirect questions back to EVA.
A simple feedback mechanism—thumbs up or down—allowed staff to rate responses

kp.k: Nevada guardianship monitoring remains a pre-launch case study
kp.d: Based on an interview with Kathleen McCloskey, the Nevada account describes a portal intended to streamline guardian reporting, integrate financial information through Plaid, and alert courts to potential fraud. Assessment following 2017 legislative changes identified inadequate monitoring and fragmented data systems. Development required migration from an initially purchased platform to a more flexible product already used by the court. User feedback was favorable, but rollout was scheduled for October 2025, so the account does not establish post-deployment fraud-detection or efficiency outcomes.
qs: Nevada’s guardianship monitoring portal uses AI to detect signs of fraud, particularly in financial reporting, and sends alerts to the court.
some courts were using sticky notes to track cases because they didn’t have any other resources.
The project is now set to roll out in October 2025.
The court also recommends inventorying what software or systems the court already uses

kp.k: Texas e-filing automation reports gains after iterative human review
kp.d: The Texas case study, based on an interview with Casey Kennedy, describes CSI/Tyler Technologies software combining AI and robotic process automation to check minimum filing standards. A limited pilot expanded across case types after staff reviewed decisions and supplied feedback. The account reports about 60% correct performance initially and later accuracy exceeding human performance, with substantial processing-time reductions, but gives no final accuracy percentage, sample size, or quantified time saving. Initial training and verification required extra staff time; review effort subsequently declined.
qs: Document Automation software by CSI/Tyler Technologies processes court filings using a combination of AI and Robotic Process Automation.
Right out of the box, CSI’s model was getting about 60% right
Now, the accuracy rate is better than human performance.
Initially, the project required extra staff time to train, test, and improve the models.

kp.k: Faster automation can increase downstream staff stress
kp.d: The Texas account reports that continuous automated filing approvals produced weekend queues that made downstream staff feel perpetually behind. The court therefore restricted processing to staff business hours despite the technology's ability to operate continuously. This illustrates the guide's recommendation to judge success through personnel experience and end-to-end workflow effects rather than throughput alone.
qs: They would arrive to work on Monday morning to find 2.5 days’ worth of filings that had been approved over the weekend and were ready for staff review.
They shared that this made them feel like they were always behind.
the court now uses the technology to process new filings during the same hours that staff are working.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Miller and the workgroup present AI as a conditional means of improving court administration, access, staff work and service delivery; the interviewed practitioners report specific operational benefits.
pts.d: The guide predicts that carefully implemented AI could improve access, fairness, efficiency and public trust, automate routine work and let personnel focus on higher-value tasks. It also identifies risks: biased data can magnify inaccuracies and bias; hybrid workflows can produce double-work; vendor dependence and model changes can create operational and legal risks. In the Orange County EVA case study, based on Darren Dang's interview, a procedural-knowledge chatbot reportedly accelerated staff readiness, improved consistency and exposed outdated procedures. The account describes the project as resource positive and predicts potentially quick returns for similar purchased tools. In Nevada, Kathleen McCloskey's account describes a portal intended to simplify guardianship reporting and flag possible financial fraud that human reviewers may miss. In Texas, Casey Kennedy's account reports that combined AI and robotic process automation reduced filing-approval time and eventually exceeded human accuracy. That automation also increased downstream staff stress when operating over weekends, leading the court to restrict operation to business hours. The guide primarily frames AI as supporting human expertise and decision-making, while recognizing that some individual tasks may be replaced altogether.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of multidisciplinary guidance and practitioner interview case studies, with limited reported quantitative results and no independently documented comparative evaluation.
pts.d: The broad benefits and risk claims are guidance informed by workgroup expertise, institutional resources and early court implementations, rather than findings from a controlled study. EVA's account reports that approximately half of entry-level staff were new or had less than two years in role. The court tracked adoption, response accuracy and completeness, usage dashboards and staff feedback, but the guide supplies no numerical outcome series and explicitly says no formal ROI analysis was conducted. Nevada's account relies on an NCSC-assisted assessment, feasibility study and user-group feedback before rollout, not post-launch fraud-detection results. Texas reportedly had baseline processing-time data and compared it with processing time after implementation, including staff review of AI decisions. Its initial model performance is described as about 60% correct; later better-than-human accuracy and time savings are reported without final percentages, sample sizes or a detailed comparison method. These are claims from Kennedy's interview account, not an independent benchmark. Separate unnamed e-filing and calendar-management examples give detailed costs and benefits, including 40% faster filing processing and 25% improved courtroom utilization, but identify neither courts nor supporting studies; they should remain distinct from the named interview case studies. The guide also supplies token-optimization savings ranges without a stated measurement basis.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Benefits are conditional on governance, data quality, human oversight and iterative implementation; the September 2025 guide distinguishes deployed projects from planned expansion and a forthcoming Nevada launch.
pts.d: The guide does not assign a profession-wide transformation deadline. It proposes a year-long foundational governance process and recommends selecting an initial project that can be implemented and evaluated within 6–12 months. Those are planning recommendations, not measured delivery times. It favors low-risk internal first projects over public-facing applications or decisions affecting sentencing and case outcomes. Successful adoption is presented as requiring appropriate data, role-specific AI literacy, stakeholder participation, verification, monitoring and maintenance. EVA had already expanded from civil procedures to other case domains, but public-facing self-help and multilingual services remained an envisioned extension. The prediction of quick ROI for a similar purchased tool is prospective and unquantified. Nevada's rollout was scheduled for October 2025, so its case study cannot establish realized post-launch outcomes. Texas's benefits emerged gradually through court-specific data, staff review and feedback, followed by expansion across case types; exact deployment dates are not given. Initial training and review required extra staff time, while continuing costs include software subscriptions and IT support. Internal-use policy excerpts are explicitly snapshots at the time of writing, not assurances of current rules.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are state-court personnel, court leadership, litigants and other court users, guardians and justice-system partners—not law-firm staffing or legal-services market segments.
pts.d: Clerks and operational staff may spend less time on repetitive processing and procedural questions, gain faster onboarding and face changed downstream workloads. Supervisors and subject-matter experts continue maintaining knowledge bases, checking performance and supporting staff. Judges retain decision-making responsibility within the guide's human-oversight framing. Court leaders and IT teams face governance, procurement, security, integration and ongoing maintenance obligations. Litigants, attorneys, unrepresented users and underserved communities could receive faster and more accessible services, although the guide treats broad access and equity gains as possibilities rather than demonstrated aggregate outcomes. Nevada's guardians may benefit from easier financial reporting, while district courts gain monitoring support. The guide does not claim lawyer displacement, changed law-firm leverage, billing-model transformation or market-share shifts. EVA's account specifically reports no need for formal staffing or recruitment changes, while the broader guide anticipates evolving AI-literacy requirements in some court roles.
